title: DNA metabarcoding reveals population‐specific links between diet and fledging success in a recovering threatened bird, the Mauritius parakeet
content:
Our findings suggest that restoration of native/endemic habitat in modified landscapes can directly improve reproductive success in a threatened endemic bird. Conservation strategies must consider the impact of dietary components on reproductive fitness. Conservation managers on Mauritius should consider prioritising protection of key endemic food plants while maintaining tailored supplementary feeding regimes based on local conditions. This approach has broad applicability for threatened species conservation in modified habitats worldwide.


Abstract

Populations of threatened species frequently persist in suboptimal landscapes comprising degraded, altered and restored habitats. Such habitat mosaics may influence diet, potentially impacting fitness. We investigated dietary variation in the Mauritius (‘echo’) parakeet (Alexandrinus eques), a threatened species that exists in two isolated populations exhibiting differing habitat quality. DNA metabarcoding of faecal samples identified plant taxa consumed, while reproductive data allowed assessment of nest-level diet-fitness relationships. We identified 83 plant taxa in 206 faecal samples and discovered significant dietary differentiation between the two populations. Despite historical declines in native vegetation across both ranges, parakeet diets in the North population contained significantly higher native species richness (4.7 vs. 1.9 species per sample). Consumption of endemic Gaertnera spp. was positively associated with reproductive success in the South, while supplementary food enhanced reproduction in the North, suggesting population-specific dietary strategies. Synthesis and applications: Our findings suggest that restoration of native/endemic habitat in modified landscapes can directly improve reproductive success in a threatened endemic bird. Conservation strategies must consider the impact of dietary components on reproductive fitness. Conservation managers on Mauritius should consider prioritising protection of key endemic food plants while maintaining tailored supplementary feeding regimes based on local conditions. This approach has broad applicability for threatened species conservation in modified habitats worldwide.
